correctness.rationale: The source definition requires all two-subsets to be distinguishable after adjoining every transformation of ranks 2 through n-1. For n=5, the proof handles every such transformation. A5 is transitive on the two orbit types of ordered distinct two-subset pairs: intersecting and disjoint. Every permitted non-permutation directly distinguishes one intersecting pair; a short fiber argument shows it also directly distinguishes one disjoint pair. Conjugating the input pair by an even permutation therefore gives a one-group-element-then-f separator for any prescribed pair. The standalone verifier checks the full quantified statement over all 3000 permitted transformations and all ordered distinct two-subset pairs.

originality.rationale: The direct 2021 source defines strong sync-maximality, proves that every 4-transitive group is strong and every strong group is primitive, and explicitly leaves proper containment open. It does not state that A5 is strongly sync-maximal or give the one-group-element separator property. Focused semantic and web searches for A5, the named strong property, 3-transitivity, rank-two witnesses, and proper containment located the defining source but no covering result. A later 2023 paper on primitive automata studies a different synchronizability question and contains no occurrence of the strong sync-maximal property.

value.rationale: The primary source explicitly asks whether strongly sync-maximal groups are properly contained between 4-transitive and primitive groups. Showing that A5 is strongly sync-maximal while not 4-transitive resolves the lower strictness half of that structural problem. The one-group-element strengthening also explains why the published 4-transitivity proof can be weakened in degree five, so the contribution is structural rather than a bare small-state computation.
